content:
Local weather is one of the most underutilized variables in your Apple Home automation setup. Over the past few years, I have used sensors to do all sorts of things, from knowing when to drip faucets to prevent water from freezing in icy conditions, to using Eve Aqua to adjust sprinkler schedules on scorching hot days. Eve Weather has been part of my setup for a while now, and after the Matter upgrade a few years back, it has proven extremely useful around my home.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips, and everything related to Apple's smart home framework.

If you have followed HomeKit Weekly for a while, you know I prefer automation that runs on its own. Smart home accessories are only useful when they can do things automatically. That's why I have always recommended building a smart home around a single ecosystem rather than mixing and matching. Even in the age of Matter, I don't want to juggle a bunch of different platforms. For me, that platform is Apple Home. I rely on Eve devices because they have always prioritized privacy, and if you stick to local control with Matter, you can avoid setting up a cloud account altogether. Eve has also actively supported Matter and Thread in recent years. This is exactly what you want to see.

Eve Weather gives you three data points in one small device: temperature, humidity, and barometric pressure. It carries an IPX4 water resistance rating, and the aluminum body looks like it naturally belongs outside my house. Mine is mounted exactly there. What it provides are hyper-localized readings, which can sometimes differ by a few degrees from what the Apple Weather app reports. Honestly, that difference matters a lot, depending on whether it's extremely hot or freezing cold. When your pipes are freezing at 31 degrees Fahrenheit, but your app shows 34, you will definitely be glad to have this local data.

One of the underrated features of Eve Weather is its built-in 12-hour weather trend display. It uses barometric pressure changes to forecast weather trends. You will see a visual icon showing whether it is likely to be sunny, cloudy, rainy, or stormy. This small detail adds a lot of value, as you can see it at a glance without having to open a phone app.

Here are a few automation examples you can set up with Eve Weather:

  • When the temperature drops below freezing, turn on a colored light to remind household members to drip the faucets.
  • When outdoor humidity is particularly high, activate a dehumidifier.
  • If it has already rained and the forecast says more rain is coming, delay the sprinkler system from running.
  • Without stepping outside, just ask Siri to tell you the current temperature in the front yard.

Matter and Thread support in 2026

A few years ago, Eve released a free firmware update that added Matter support to Eve Weather. If you already own this device, you can perform the upgrade through the Eve app. The Matter version supports Amazon Alexa, Google Home, and SmartThings, as well as Apple Home. The sensor itself remains exactly the same — it has simply become cross-platform, so you won't have to worry if you decide to switch to another major smart home ecosystem in the future.

Eve Weather is what's called a "Thread end device." That means it communicates via Thread but does not relay data. That job is left to "Full Thread Devices" that are always powered on, such as the Eve Energy or Eve Water Guard. The more "Full Thread Devices" you have, the stronger and more stable your Thread network becomes, and battery-powered devices like Eve Weather directly benefit from that stability.

You still don't need an Eve account. Unless you opt in yourself, everything stays local. Eve's iPhone app is an excellent tool that lets you visualize and track historical trends for temperature, barometric pressure, and humidity. This is genuinely a great way to spot patterns and make smarter decisions about things like watering the lawn or managing energy usage.

I have several HomePod minis placed around my house, and I also rely on my Eero 6E network to support Thread. Eero's software has Thread support built in, so for accessories like Eve Weather, it provides a solid foundation to stay connected and run smoothly.

Wrap-up after using Eve Weather

The only thing I would still love to see is a rechargeable battery. The battery lasts for several months, but I would much prefer a USB-C port like the one on Eve Room. That said, Eve Weather remains one of my favorite Apple Home accessories. It is simple, looks good, and thanks to Matter, it works well across all major platforms. If you plan to bring local weather information into your smart home and set up some practical automations, Eve Weather is an easy recommendation for me.

You can buy it from Amazon or directly from the Eve Store.
